mustMemoriseRules: chromatography → separation based on different distributions between a stationary phase and a mobile phase
stationary phase → the phase that does not move during chromatography
mobile phase → the solvent phase moving through the stationary phase
greater solvent movement → the result for a component more soluble in the mobile phase and less attracted to the stationary phase
pure chromatogram spot → one spot produced by a pure substance under a given set of conditions
mixture chromatogram → a chromatogram that may show more than one spot
Rf equation → distance moved by substance divided by distance moved by solvent front
Rf unit → no unit because Rf is a ratio of two distances in the same unit
Rf range → normally from 0 to 1 inclusive
pencil baseline → a starting line that will not dissolve and travel with the solvent

detailedExplanation: Verified against The Tiffin Girls’ School Year 9 Chemistry Curriculum Outline 2026–27 (AQA GCSE Chemistry 8462).

Paper chromatography separates substances because they have different attractions to the stationary phase and different solubilities in the mobile phase. Substances that travel different distances can form separate spots.

The baseline is drawn in pencil because graphite does not dissolve in the solvent in the same way as many inks. The sample spots must start above the solvent level so they do not simply dissolve into the solvent reservoir.

Rf = distance moved by substance ÷ distance moved by solvent front. An Rf value is between 0 and 1. For identification, comparisons should be made using the same solvent and similar experimental conditions.
For reproducibility, repeat the method or compare independent results under the same conditions. Close agreement increases confidence that the result is reproducible.

Chromatography separates components of a mixture because they distribute differently between a stationary phase and a mobile phase. In paper chromatography, the solvent moves up the paper. Components that are more soluble in the mobile phase and less attracted to the stationary phase tend to move further.
A pure substance produces one spot under a given set of conditions; a mixture may produce more than one.
